contexts.title: What the bill does
contexts.html: The bill creates federal rules for "stablecoins". These are digital coins. The company issuing them (the issuer) must redeem them for a fixed dollar value, which means exchanging them for money. Only permitted, regulated companies may issue these coins. Each coin must be fully backed one-to-one by cash or similar safe assets. Issuers may not lend those assets out. The bill also sets rules for repaying users and requires approved issuers to follow lawful orders to block payments.

Here, “that subsection” means subsection (a) of section 507 of title 11, the federal bankruptcy law.

contexts.title: The bankruptcy pause on redemptions
contexts.html:
The automatic stay is a bankruptcy rule. It pauses actions to collect money from a failed company until a court allows them. CRS describes this as a power to “allow a bankruptcy court to issue automatic stays on stablecoin redemptions.” [SEP 1] During a pause, a holder may have a legal claim but no spendable money. CRS is the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress.

Lawyers write: “Section 11(c) of the proposed Act applies the automatic stay to actions against the reserves.” [UNC 38]

The same lawyers say the bill “provides an accelerated procedure for stablecoin holders to obtain relief from the automatic stay” [UNC 38]. But “the court shall use best efforts to enter a final order to begin distributions under this paragraph not later than 14 days after the date of the required hearing.” [UNC 3] This is a best-efforts target. It runs from a hearing and concerns beginning payouts, not finishing them.

contexts.title: Duties to block payments and obey lawful orders
contexts.html:
To block or freeze means to stop coins from moving. Issuers can do this because they control the software of their coins. A lawful order is a final, valid requirement under federal law from a court or authorized agency.

Section 4 requires “technical capabilities, policies, and procedures to block, freeze, and reject specific or impermissible transactions that violate Federal or State laws, rules, or regulations” [UNN 2].

Section 4 also says: “A permitted payment stablecoin issuer may issue payment stablecoins only if the issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order.” [SES 4] Such orders require an issuer to “seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person” [SES 4]. They must be “issued or promulgated under Federal law” [UNN 2] and specify “the payment stablecoins or accounts subject to blocking with reasonable particularity” [UNN 2].

The law firm Steptoe writes: “However, the GENIUS Act now makes such capabilities a legal prerequisite for operation.” [UNT 8] Here, “such capabilities” means some central control over the coins, such as an ability to blacklist wallet addresses or burn tokens. Freezing reaches tokens “held by persons with no relationship to the issuer and regardless of whether the tokens are in a custodial or non-custodial wallet.” [UNT 8] A non-custodial wallet is one a person controls without a company holding the coins.

A foreign issuer is based outside the United States. A digital asset service provider is a firm, such as a U.S. trading platform, that offers crypto to customers. The secondary market is where people trade coins with each other rather than with the issuer.

Section 8: a foreign coin may not be offered through these providers “unless the foreign payment stablecoin issuer has the technological capability to comply and complies with the terms of any lawful order.” [UNN 2]

Section 3 has a similar condition: “unless the foreign payment stablecoin issuer has the technological capability to comply, and will comply, with the terms of any lawful order and any reciprocal arrangement pursuant to section 18.” [UNT 3]

If an issuer defies an order, Treasury can issue a notice “prohibiting digital asset service providers from facilitating secondary trading of payment stablecoins issued by the foreign payment stablecoin issuer in the United States.” [UNN 2]

contexts.title: Consumer rules for issuers
contexts.html:
Issuers must publish procedures for “timely redemption of outstanding payment stablecoins” [3]. Redemption means exchanging a coin for money. Discretionary limits require a regulator's decision: “any discretionary limitations on timely redemptions can only be imposed by a State qualified payment stablecoin regulator, the Corporation, the Comptroller, or the Board” [3]. These are a state regulator or a federal banking regulator: the FDIC (“the Corporation”), the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (“the Comptroller”) or the Federal Reserve (“the Board”).

Purchase and cash-out fees must be disclosed in plain language, and “such fees can only be changed upon not less than 7 days' prior notice to consumers” [3].

Issuers must “publish the monthly composition of the issuer's reserves on the website of the issuer” [3]. This means listing what the reserves are made of. Monthly reports must be “examined by a registered public accounting firm.” [3]

Senior executives must submit “a certification as to the accuracy of the monthly report” [3]. This makes named managers answer for the information users receive.

The bill bans false claims of government backing or insurance: “It shall be unlawful to represent that payment stablecoins are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, guaranteed by the United States Government, or subject to Federal deposit insurance or Federal share insurance.” [3]

The bill excludes managers convicted of specified crimes: “The bill would prohibit anyone who has been convicted of certain financial crimes of being an officer or director of an issuer.” [4]

Federal licensing reviews must assess “The competence, experience, and integrity of the officers, directors, and principal shareholders of the applicant” [3].

Federal regulators can order a violating issuer to “take affirmative action to correct the conditions resulting from any such violation or practice.” [3] State regulators receive “supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority over all State qualified payment stablecoin issuers of such State.” [3]

An issuer may not condition service on buying “an additional paid product or service from the permitted payment stablecoin issuer, or any of its subsidiaries” [3] or on agreeing “to not obtain an additional product or service from a competitor.” [3]

nodes.title: The bill would increase stablecoin use overall
nodes.claim_html: Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, S.1582’s national rules and clearer legal permission would tend to increase the issuance or use of payment stablecoins at least somewhat. This claim does not say how much, how fast, or who the new users would be.

nodes.title: Added use would reach households’ everyday money
nodes.claim_html: Some of the added stablecoin use would come from ordinary households keeping or spending everyday money in payment stablecoins, as a substitute for cash or bank transaction accounts. This claim does not say how much or how soon.

nodes.title: The bill would lead to more Bitcoin mining
nodes.claim_html: By expanding and legitimizing stablecoins and crypto, S.1582 would tend to lead to more Bitcoin mining than would happen without it. This claim does not say how much more.

nodes.title: More mining would add climate pollution
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, the added mining would add greenhouse gas pollution, from power plants that supply mines and from electricity bought from the grid.

nodes.title: More mining would add air pollution that causes acid rain
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, the added mining would add nitrogen oxides from power plants that supply mines. These gases help form acid rain.

nodes.title: More mining would add pressure on scarce freshwater
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, the added mining would consume more freshwater through cooling and electricity production, including in drought-prone or resource-scarce areas.

nodes.title: More mining would add harm to fish and water from power-plant cooling
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, power plants that supply the added mining would take and return more cooling water, harming fish, wildlife and water quality.

nodes.title: More mining would add land damage and waste from its power supply
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, generating its added electricity would add solid waste from burning fossil fuels and land damage from fuel extraction.

nodes.title: More mining would add discarded equipment that can pollute
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, the added mining would discard more single-purpose mining chips, adding electronic waste that can pollute air and water when poorly disposed of.

nodes.title: More mining would add noise near wildlife
nodes.claim_html: If mining grows, the added mines would add fan noise in rural places, putting nearby wildlife at risk.

nodes.title: Clearer rules would bring faster stablecoin settlement to renewable-energy markets
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s clearer legal permission would lead some institutions in renewable-energy and carbon markets, such as corporate energy buyers and project developers, to settle trades in stablecoins, releasing money sooner than legacy payment systems do.

nodes.title: Faster settlement would help get renewable power built
nodes.claim_html: Money released sooner by faster settlement would modestly improve the finances of renewable-energy projects, including some that can only barely get built, so that at least some renewable power would be built or used that otherwise would not be.

nodes.title: Backing rules would make permitted coins more likely to be repaid in full
nodes.claim_html: Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, the bill’s backing and reserve-use rules would make it less likely that a permitted issuer’s coins could not be repaid at their full promised value.

nodes.title: Failure rules would let holders recover more of their money
nodes.claim_html: If a permitted issuer, or a firm holding coins or reserves for customers, fails, the bill’s holder priority, its exclusion of reserves from the bankruptcy estate and its custody rules would let holders recover more of their money than under the law in force on July 17, 2025.

nodes.title: Failure rules would get usable payment money back to holders sooner
nodes.claim_html: When a permitted issuer fails, the bill’s priority rules and its court route to prompt distributions would get usable payment money back to holders sooner, limiting the disruption the failure causes to households, businesses and commerce.

nodes.title: Reserve and oversight rules would make runs and forced sales less likely
nodes.claim_html: Compared with the law in force on July 17, 2025, the bill’s backing, reserve-use, diversification, reporting and oversight rules would make runs on permitted coins, and the forced sales of reserve assets that can spread them, less likely.

nodes.title: Required IT standards would make issuers’ systems safer
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s required operational and information-technology risk standards would make permitted issuers’ own systems less exposed to theft, cyberattacks and payment failures than they would otherwise be.

nodes.title: Household money in stablecoins could lose value without insurance
nodes.claim_html: Some household money moved into permitted stablecoins could lose value, because the coins are not insured, can trade below $1 where ordinary customers use them, and can be backed by assets that lose value or are taken first by a lender.

nodes.title: Household money could be frozen if an issuer fails
nodes.claim_html: If a permitted issuer failed, the bankruptcy pause on redemptions would leave some households’ everyday money in its coins unavailable to spend until a court allowed payments.

nodes.title: Stablecoin payers would lack refund rights after theft or mistakes
nodes.claim_html: Households paying with permitted stablecoins would lack enforceable rights to refunds and help after unauthorized transfers or payment mistakes that people paying by card or bank transfer have.

nodes.title: Small holders would face costly or unequal cash-out
nodes.claim_html: Households holding small amounts of permitted coins would depend on middlemen and face redemption fees with no cap, unequal terms and minimums they cannot meet when turning coins back into money.

nodes.title: Official approval would draw household money into scams
nodes.claim_html: The credibility of official approval would draw some household money into coins used by scammers, adding to fraud losses.

nodes.title: Network failure can interrupt payments despite safe reserves
nodes.claim_html: Stablecoins can run on shared networks that the issuer does not control, and a network failure or outage can interrupt payments even when reserves are safe. This claim makes no statement about attack incentives and is not an adoption forecast.

nodes.title: Ethereum activity raises the incentive to attack
nodes.claim_html: On Ethereum, under assumed growth in stablecoin activity, the reward for an attack rises without a matching rise in its cost or punishment. The source says the likelihood of these attacks may remain low under normal conditions. This claim concerns incentives, not a stated likelihood of attack, and it is not an adoption forecast.

nodes.title: Everyday payment money would come to depend on networks that can fail
nodes.claim_html: Some households’ everyday payment money, including money needed for essentials such as medical care, would come to depend on shared public networks, so that an outage there could leave it unusable for a time.

nodes.title: Money for essentials would face a rising attack incentive
nodes.claim_html: Some households’ payment money needed for essentials, including medical care, would come to be held or spent on Ethereum, where growth in stablecoin activity raises the reward for attacking the payments it carries. That money would therefore face a greater incentive-driven risk of being cut off by an attack. This claim does not say how often attacks would happen or that one would succeed.

nodes.title: Runs on stablecoins can pull money out of banks
nodes.claim_html: Because reserves may be held as bank deposits, including uninsured deposits, a rush to redeem stablecoins can pull money out of banks. This claim concerns that mechanism, not its expected size. The reverse direction, from bank trouble to a stablecoin run, is background and is not part of this claim.

nodes.title: Serious financial shocks can reach people who never used stablecoins
nodes.claim_html: A serious financial shock, including the failure of a major stablecoin issuer or crypto firm, can harm people who never used stablecoins through their pensions, savings, jobs or loans. This claim concerns who can be reached, not the size or likelihood of a shock.

nodes.title: Forced sales in a run would spread stress to banks
nodes.claim_html: With added use, forced sales of reserve assets during a stablecoin run could spread stress to the banking system.

nodes.title: Mass cash-outs would push up federal borrowing costs
nodes.claim_html: With added use, mass cash-outs from stablecoins would force sales of short-term Treasury debt and put upward pressure on the federal government’s short-term borrowing costs.

nodes.title: A stablecoin panic would bring pressure for a public rescue
nodes.claim_html: With added use, a spreading stablecoin panic would put pressure on regulators to step in with public support, whose cost could fall on people who never used stablecoins.

nodes.title: Stablecoin growth would reduce deposit funding for local lending
nodes.claim_html: If stablecoin use grows, some money would leave deposits at lenders that rely on local deposits. This would leave those lenders with less funding for loans. Issuers themselves cannot replace those loans. This claim does not say how much or name any one lender.

nodes.title: Lost loan funding would fall hardest in poor and rural places
nodes.claim_html: That loss of loan funding would fall especially on borrowers in rural and low-income areas, where community banks supply home, farm and small-business loans.

nodes.title: Less local lending would cost jobs
nodes.claim_html: That loss of loan funding would mean scarcer loans for local businesses and farms, weaker investment and fewer jobs.

nodes.title: Less deposit funding would reach lenders that serve churches
nodes.claim_html: That loss of deposit funding would reach lenders that fund churches and ministries, such as Christian credit unions, reducing their lending.

nodes.title: The ban on issuer interest removes one pull on bank deposits
nodes.claim_html: S.1582’s ban on issuer interest removes one incentive that could otherwise draw money away from bank deposits that support lending. The claim concerns payments by issuers; it does not say all rewards are barred.

nodes.title: Blocking duties would stop some identified illegal payments
nodes.claim_html: Compared with prior practice, the bill’s duties to block payments and obey lawful orders, for permitted issuers and for foreign issuers whose coins U.S. platforms trade, would stop at least some identified illegal payments that would otherwise have gone through. This claim does not concern how payments are identified.

nodes.title: Reporting duties would help identify illegal payments
nodes.claim_html: Compared with prior law, the Section 4 monitoring and reporting duties would help issuers or investigators identify at least some illegal stablecoin payments involving an issuer’s own account holders that they would otherwise miss. This claim does not say the duties reach secondary-market transfers between other people, and it does not concern the legal power to stop a known payment.

nodes.title: Section 9 would lead to monitoring beyond issuers’ own dealings
nodes.claim_html: Section 9(d) requires FinCEN to write standards for issuers’ systems to monitor blockchain transactions, and this would likely lead issuers to watch at least some transfers beyond their direct dealings. The rules are unwritten; this claim does not require a specific final rule.

nodes.title: The bill would disrupt some fentanyl-ingredient purchases and the poisonous pills they supply
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s tools would disrupt at least some stablecoin purchases of fentanyl ingredients and equipment, and so reduce the supply of fake pills that poison people in the United States.

nodes.title: The bill would deny ransomware attackers some of their profits
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s tools would find or freeze at least some ransomware profits moved in stablecoins, reducing attacks that delay hospital care and emergency services.

nodes.title: The bill would cut off some terrorist funds
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s added pressure on issuers to carry out freezes would cut off at least some stablecoin funds of terrorist groups such as ISIS.

nodes.title: Cutting off those funds would reduce violence in the United States
nodes.claim_html: Cutting off those terrorist funds would reduce support for attacks in the United States and for the promotion of such attacks.

nodes.title: The bill would disrupt some investment-scam networks
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s tools would find or cut off funds of at least some investment-scam networks that take stablecoins, before they take more from victims.

nodes.title: The bill would disrupt some sexual-blackmail payments
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s tools would find or freeze at least some stablecoin payments to sexual blackmailers, reducing coercion that drives victims to despair and suicide.

nodes.title: The bill would preserve some stolen money for victims
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s tools would freeze or seize at least some stolen stablecoins before they move beyond recovery, so that they can be returned to victims.

nodes.title: The bill would help the state trace and cut off threat financing
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s licensing screens, reporting, blocking duties and conditions on foreign issuers would help U.S. authorities find and interrupt more funding for terrorists, cartels and other security threats than under the law in force on July 17, 2025.

nodes.title: Added use would move more threat funding beyond identity checks
nodes.claim_html: With added use, more payments by terrorists, sanctions evaders and criminal networks would move through stablecoin transfers beyond identity checks, making them harder for authorities to stop.

nodes.title: The foreign-issuer route would expose U.S. payments to hidden adversary control
nodes.claim_html: With added use, the bill’s route for foreign issuers would let issuers under hidden control of foreign adversaries carry more U.S. payments, because it does not require rigorous screening of foreign government ties.

nodes.title: Identity checks would lead issuers to reject Muslim and Arab customers as high risk
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s more detailed customer checks would lead some issuers to reject customers, such as Muslim and Arab, Middle Eastern and South Asian Americans, whose religious giving or family payments abroad look risky.

nodes.title: Identity checks would exclude people whose documents do not fit
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s identity-verification duties would lead some issuers to turn away people whose documents or life histories do not fit the usual process, such as refugees, Indigenous people with tribal IDs, and people who have changed their name or gender.

nodes.title: Wider monitoring would deter support for unpopular groups
nodes.claim_html: If issuers monitor transfers beyond their own dealings, linking donations and dues to identified people would deter some support for and contact with unpopular groups.

nodes.title: Wider use would move church gifts onto traceable records
nodes.claim_html: With added use, some church gifts would move from cash onto stablecoin transfers that can be traced back to identified accounts.

nodes.title: The bill leaves commercial companies a more usable route
nodes.claim_html: S.1582 does not bar commercial companies from issuing stablecoins. Privately held commercial companies do not face the special committee test. By removing regulatory uncertainty, the bill makes this existing route more usable. Such firms still need an issuer license.

nodes.title: Commercial platforms could make their payment systems hard to leave
nodes.claim_html: Nonfinancial firms involved in stablecoin payments could use their existing data or other businesses to raise the costs of switching to other payment products, making those payment systems hard to leave. This claim concerns the possibility, not any one firm.

nodes.title: Commercial platforms would pressure sellers who depend on them
nodes.claim_html: Commercial platforms that issue stablecoins would use their other businesses to press small sellers and workers who depend on them for income into using their payment products.

nodes.title: Commercial platforms would concentrate control over essential payments
nodes.claim_html: Commercial platforms would build stablecoin payment systems that become hard to leave, concentrating control over essential payments in a few private firms.

nodes.title: Commercial issuers would use payment data to steer customers
nodes.claim_html: Commercial companies issuing stablecoins would use customers’ payment data to steer them toward more expensive choices.

nodes.title: The tying ban and standards power would lower switching barriers
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s ban on tying and its power to set compatibility standards would lower the barriers that make stablecoin payment systems hard to leave.

nodes.title: Wider use would benefit the President’s family business, and ethics rules do not stop that
nodes.claim_html: The President’s family has a stablecoin business that stands to benefit if the bill widens stablecoin use, and the ethics provisions the bill relies on do not bar the President from owning or running it. This claim does not say any official act has been influenced.

nodes.title: A larger family business would give outside interests more ways to enrich the President
nodes.claim_html: A larger stablecoin business would give interested parties, including foreign ones, more ways to enrich the President’s family, for example by choosing and holding its coin.

nodes.title: More dollar tokens would keep more payments within U.S. reach
nodes.claim_html: With added use, growth in regulated dollar stablecoins would keep more international payments within reach of U.S. financial controls, against rival systems designed to escape them.

nodes.title: Reserve demand would lower the government’s net borrowing costs
nodes.claim_html: With added use, demand for Treasury bills from stablecoin reserves would lower the federal government’s short-term borrowing costs, net of any fall in other demand for that debt and in public earnings from issuing money.

nodes.title: Dollar tokens would destabilize vulnerable foreign economies
nodes.claim_html: With added use, people in countries with volatile currencies would move from their own money into dollar stablecoins, making money flee faster and weakening those countries’ control of their own economies.

nodes.title: Replacing cash would shift public income to issuers
nodes.claim_html: With added use, stablecoins replacing public currency would shift income from issuing money away from the U.S. Treasury and foreign governments to private issuers.

nodes.title: The framework would keep payment firms and expertise in the United States
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s domestic framework would keep stablecoin firms and expertise in the United States that would otherwise move abroad, supporting U.S. capacity to build and oversee this payment technology.

nodes.title: The framework would give online betting businesses a clearer payment route
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s framework would give online betting businesses a clearer, more reliable route to receive payments in compliant stablecoins.

nodes.title: The framework would give pornography businesses a clearer payment route
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s framework would give pornography businesses a clearer, more reliable route to receive payments in compliant stablecoins.

nodes.title: A nationwide license would bring new providers of bankless and low-cost transfers
nodes.claim_html: By replacing extra state licenses for federally approved issuers, the bill would let more new providers, banks and nonbanks, offer stablecoin payments nationwide, widening access to bankless payments and lower-cost international transfers for people such as migrant families and small firms.

nodes.title: The committee test would keep a commercial group’s financial trouble from spreading
nodes.claim_html: For public companies mainly outside finance, the bill’s requirement of unanimous committee approval would reduce the chance that trouble on the financial side of such a company spreads to its other businesses, to banks or to ordinary commerce.

nodes.title: Limits on issuers’ activities would keep stablecoin trouble from spreading
nodes.claim_html: Restricting issuers to offering and redeeming stablecoins and supporting activities would reduce the routes through which an issuer’s trouble spreads into banking and ordinary commerce.

nodes.title: A failure of one state’s supervision would spread nationwide and be hard to contain
nodes.claim_html: Because issuers under one state’s supervision can operate nationally, a failure of that state’s supervision would expose payments across the country, and the conditional federal backup would make that threat harder to contain quickly than one confined to that state.

nodes.title: Nature: stronger legal tools against payments for crimes that destroy nature
nodes.claim_html: The bill makes freezing a legal duty for permitted issuers and makes a foreign issuer’s access to U.S. trading services depend on obeying lawful orders. For payments in covered coins that a lawful U.S. order identifies, these are stronger enforceable means to interrupt payments and seize proceeds from crimes such as illegal gold mining and wildlife trafficking, which destroy forests and wildlife. Either legal tool is enough on its own. Giving authorities stronger tools against those crimes serves the wish to defend nature, even though how often the tools would be used, and how much they would add to issuers’ earlier voluntary freezes, is uncertain.

nodes.title: Nature: protecting donations used to defend forests
nodes.claim_html: Stablecoin gifts to forest defenders such as Rainforest Foundation US are protected while they are held as approved coins, whether through safer backing or stronger recovery if an issuer fails. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting this way of giving preserves money for forest defense and helps people take part in defending nature.

nodes.title: Nature: more renewable power
nodes.claim_html: More renewable power being built or used cuts climate pollution, because renewables have much lower life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions than fossil fuels. That protects nature from pollution.

nodes.title: Nature: harms from more Bitcoin mining
nodes.claim_html: More mining can harm nature in several ways: climate pollution, air pollution that causes acid rain, pressure on scarce freshwater, cooling-water harm to fish, land damage and waste from its power supply, discarded equipment, and noise near wildlife. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting forests, water and wildlife from that harm gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: safer money for people with little cushion
nodes.claim_html: Coins more likely to be repaid in full protect small savings and aid payments, including money that vulnerable people abroad need for food, shelter and care. People with little financial cushion are least able to absorb a loss. That serves concern for vulnerable people.

nodes.title: Concern: just treatment of customers when a firm fails
nodes.claim_html: Stronger recovery rights, if you accepted them, and a regulator required to speak for customers in an issuer’s reorganization give customers protection they lack the power to bargain for themselves. Either is enough on its own. That supports just treatment of customers.

nodes.title: Concern: consumer safeguards in the bill
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s cash-out rules and fee notices, checked reserve reports and truthful-marketing rules, screening of managers with public enforcement, and ban on forced purchases protect customers who cannot investigate or challenge a firm themselves. If you accepted that the required IT standards make issuers’ systems safer, that protection counts too. Any one of these serves concern for vulnerable people and fair treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting people who never use stablecoins
nodes.claim_html: If runs are less likely and shocks can reach people who never used stablecoins, reducing those runs protects strangers’ pensions, savings and credit. That extends concern to people who never chose to use stablecoins.

nodes.title: Concern: stolen money returned to victims
nodes.claim_html: Preserving stolen money so that it can be returned to its owners serves justice for victims, including people across borders whom one will never meet.

nodes.title: Concern: a say over commercial use of payment data
nodes.claim_html: Requiring consent before covered companies use, sell or share private payment data for commercial ends gives customers a say over their private financial lives. That supports just treatment.

nodes.title: Concern: wider access to payments for people who need them
nodes.claim_html: More providers offering bankless payments and lower-cost transfers would widen financial opportunity for migrant families, households receiving money from abroad and small firms. That advances equal opportunity.

nodes.title: Concern: fair treatment of license applicants
nodes.claim_html: Stated approval criteria, reasons for rejection and a right to appeal require officials to treat applicants fairly. That supports just treatment by public officials.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting community lending
nodes.claim_html: Removing one pull on deposits protects money that community banks lend to households and small firms, especially in rural and low-income areas where limited credit already restricts opportunity.

nodes.title: Concern: essential money lost or out of reach
nodes.claim_html: Household money in stablecoins could be lost, frozen, or stolen without a refund. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Money needed for food, rent and other necessities that is lost or out of reach harms people without a cash cushion, who are least able to absorb it. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: unequal and costly cash-out for small holders
nodes.claim_html: Small holders who must rely on middlemen, uncapped fees and terms they cannot meet are treated less fairly than large customers who redeem directly. That gives a reason, from fair treatment, to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: weaker checks on issuers and sellers
nodes.claim_html: Removing permitted coins from the commodity regulator’s fraud law, or letting nationwide approval take effect without a completed safety decision or another state’s license, weakens protection for people who cannot check a firm themselves. Either is enough on its own.

nodes.title: Concern: no share of the money’s earnings for holders
nodes.claim_html: The interest ban stops direct holders from bargaining for a share of what their money earns while they bear its uninsured risk. That works against fair treatment of ordinary holders.

nodes.title: Concern: workers owed wages paid after token holders
nodes.claim_html: When required reserves are missing, paying token holders first leaves less for workers already owed wages. Treating those workers’ claims justly gives a reason to oppose this change.

nodes.title: Concern: fewer loans in poor and rural communities
nodes.claim_html: Fewer home, farm and small-business loans in poor and rural communities threaten people’s chances to build a livelihood. That gives a reason, from concern for equal opportunity, to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: strangers bearing private payment risks
nodes.claim_html: A run that reaches banks, forced sales that spread stress, or a public rescue would carry private firms’ risks to uninvolved workers, retirees, borrowers and taxpayers. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting people from risks they never chose gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: pressure on people who depend on platforms for income
nodes.claim_html: Payment terms that small sellers and workers cannot refuse without risking their income work against equal opportunity. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: payment data used to steer customers
nodes.claim_html: Sellers using customers’ financial information to steer them toward more expensive choices exercise unequal power over them. Protecting customers from that power gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: privileged access to public power
nodes.claim_html: More ways for interested parties to enrich the President give wealthy interests another route to seek favor. Just treatment of everyone, including people without that access, gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: instability in vulnerable foreign economies
nodes.claim_html: Faster capital flight and weaker tools for stabilizing their own economies would harm people in poorer and more volatile countries. Concern for vulnerable people everywhere gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: less public income for shared needs
nodes.claim_html: Less public income from issuing money leaves less for shared services, especially in countries already short of tax revenue. Protecting the people who depend on those services gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Concern: the public paying to oversee private payments
nodes.claim_html: The public, including people who never use stablecoins, pays part of the cost of overseeing this private payment business. Fair treatment gives a reason to oppose placing those costs on the public.

nodes.title: Tolerance: hearing applicants who challenge a refusal
nodes.claim_html: Requiring officials to judge applicants by safety and to hear them when they disagree with a refusal puts listening to people who disagree into practice. That gives a reason, from tolerance, to support the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: protecting a payment route for unpopular voices
nodes.claim_html: Protecting funds on a payment route that works without the approval of payment companies, banks or authoritarian governments protects a means that people with unpopular views use to speak, organize and support one another. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Accepting people despite disagreement gives a reason to support the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: payment choices for migrants and displaced people
nodes.claim_html: Protecting coins that migrants and displaced people use, and requiring clear issuer fees, make room for cross-border family ties and people’s own choices about receiving help. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Accepting people whose lives differ gives a reason to support the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: control over payment data that reveals beliefs
nodes.claim_html: Letting users refuse covered issuers permission to turn payment records into advertising profiles, or to pass them to outsiders, protects people’s ability to keep different beliefs and associations without those differences becoming grounds for unfair treatment.

nodes.title: Tolerance: excluding people because of who they are
nodes.claim_html: Identity checks can lead issuers to reject Muslim and Arab customers as high risk, or to turn away people whose documents do not fit. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Accepting people across religious, cultural and personal differences gives a reason to resist excluding them, and so to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: deterring support for unpopular groups
nodes.claim_html: Deterring the private support and contact that let unpopular groups speak and be heard works against listening to and understanding different people. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tolerance: easier financial exclusion over disputed judicial work
nodes.claim_html: Required freezing powers make it easier to enforce financial penalties against International Criminal Court judges and others for judicial work the U.S. government rejects. Accepting people despite disagreement gives a reason to resist cutting them off from ordinary payments.

nodes.title: Personal Security: fewer harms from crimes paid in stablecoins
nodes.claim_html: Fewer fatal poisonings from fake pills, fewer ransomware delays to hospital care, less terrorist violence in the United States, less scam harm to mental health, or less sexual blackmail would make an average American safer. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own.

nodes.title: Personal Security: money for medical care lost or out of reach
nodes.claim_html: Household money needed for medical care could be lost, frozen in a failure, cut off by a network outage, placed at greater risk from attack, or hit by a financial shock that reaches people who never used stablecoins. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Losing access to money for care, or a greater risk of losing it, threatens an average American’s health, because cost already keeps many people from care.

nodes.title: Personal Security: financial strain linked to depression
nodes.claim_html: Fraud losses, or a financial shock reaching people who never used stablecoins, can leave people struggling to pay bills. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. That financial strain is linked to depression, which threatens an average American’s mental health.

nodes.title: Societal Security: cutting off threat financing
nodes.claim_html: Better means to trace and interrupt funding for terrorists, cartels and other threats strengthen the state’s defense of its citizens.

nodes.title: Societal Security: fewer routes to financial crisis
nodes.claim_html: Fewer runs and forced sales, faster access to payment money after a failure, less pull on bank deposits, a committee test that keeps a commercial group’s financial trouble from spreading, or activity limits that keep an issuer’s trouble from spreading would reduce routes to a financial crisis. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting the country’s economic stability gives a reason to support the bill.

nodes.title: Societal Security: payments that keep working under threat
nodes.claim_html: Issuer systems better defended against failures and cyberattacks help keep U.S. commerce working under threat.

nodes.title: Societal Security: payments not locked inside one company
nodes.claim_html: Lower barriers to leaving a payment system keep money and commerce from being locked inside one company’s services, which supports national economic stability.

nodes.title: Societal Security: U.S. capacity in payment technology
nodes.claim_html: Keeping payment firms and expertise at home strengthens the country’s capacity to build and oversee technology central to its financial power, which supports a state able to defend its citizens.

nodes.title: Societal Security: payments within U.S. reach
nodes.claim_html: Keeping more international payments within reach of U.S. financial controls strengthens the state’s ability to use financial restrictions against security threats.

nodes.title: Societal Security: lower government borrowing costs
nodes.claim_html: Lower net borrowing costs leave more public money available to defend citizens and meet national emergencies.

nodes.title: Societal Security: threat funding beyond identity checks
nodes.claim_html: Payments that authorities find harder to stop make it harder to cut off funding for threats to Americans and to enforce U.S. sanctions.

nodes.title: Societal Security: hidden foreign control of payments
nodes.claim_html: Hidden foreign influence over payment infrastructure the country needs threatens national security.

nodes.title: Societal Security: essential payments exposed to network failure
nodes.claim_html: Essential payments that depend on networks that can fail, or that offer rising rewards for attack, put at risk transactions the country needs to keep working. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own.

nodes.title: Societal Security: runs that spread into banks, markets and commerce
nodes.claim_html: A run that drains banks, pressure on federal borrowing costs, frozen payment funds after a failure, or pressure for public rescues would leave the U.S. government facing financial disruption. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting the country’s stability gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Societal Security: lost credit and jobs
nodes.claim_html: Scarcer loans, weaker investment and lost jobs weaken the productive communities on which a stable, resilient country depends.

nodes.title: Societal Security: one state’s supervision with national reach
nodes.claim_html: A failure of one state’s supervision that exposes payments across the country, and that the conditional federal backup makes harder to contain quickly, threatens the country’s ability to protect its payments from a fast threat. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Societal Security: concentrated private control of payments
nodes.claim_html: Concentrating control over essential payments in a few private firms exposes the country’s payments to their business choices.

nodes.title: Societal Security: foreign rewards to a President’s business
nodes.claim_html: Giving the person who directs U.S. policy a private financial reason to please foreign interests threatens the security of the state.

nodes.title: Tradition: protecting gifts that sustain church life
nodes.claim_html: Gifts held in approved coins are protected, whether through safer backing or stronger recovery if an issuer fails. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own. Protecting money given regularly to sustain worship, teaching and missions helps congregations continue inherited religious practices.

nodes.title: Tradition: private religious giving
nodes.claim_html: Church gifts moved onto traceable records are exposed to wider scrutiny, against an inherited practice of giving privately. That gives a reason to oppose the bill.

nodes.title: Tradition: payments for betting or pornography
nodes.claim_html: A clearer payment route for online betting or for pornography strengthens a business that the Southern Baptist tradition teaches families and churches to oppose. Each consequence listed here that you accepted is enough on its own.

nodes.title: Tradition: lending that supports churches
nodes.claim_html: Less funding for lenders that serve churches and ministries threatens institutions through which families practice and pass on their faith.

glossary.definition: A digital coin that its issuer must exchange for a fixed dollar value.
The company that creates a stablecoin and must redeem it.
The cash or similar safe assets an issuer must hold to back its coins.
To exchange a coin with its issuer for money.
